name: How Contexts Fail / How to Fix Your Context (Drew Breunig)
publisher: Drew Breunig, independent writer/data scientist (dbreunig.com), formerly of Overture Maps Foundation and Reddit per task brief; no vendor affiliation identified in the essays themselves
date_published: "How Long Contexts Fail" published June 22, 2025 at https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html; follow-up "How to Fix Your Context" published June 26, 2025 at https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/26/how-to-fix-your-context.html
claim_value: Essay 1 names and defines four distinct ways a long/accumulated LLM context window degrades agent performance: Context Poisoning (a hallucination or error enters context and is repeatedly re-referenced, illustrated by Google's Gemini 2.5 Pokemon-playing agent fixating on a corrupted 'goals' section), Context Distraction (as context grows past roughly 100k tokens, the model over-relies on accumulated history over its training knowledge, shown by the same Gemini agent favoring repeated actions), Context Confusion (superfluous information degrades response quality, evidenced by the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard where a quantized Llama 3.1 8B succeeded with 19 tool definitions but failed with 46), and Context Clash (conflicting information within the assembled context actively hurts reasoning, citing a Microsoft/Salesforce study where sharding a single prompt into multi-turn delivery caused a 39% average performance drop, with OpenAI's o3 falling from 98.1 to 64.1). Essay 2 proposes six concrete mitigation tactics: RAG, Tool Loadout (keeping tool counts low, citing the same <30-tools finding), Context Quarantine (isolating subtasks into separate agent threads/contexts), Context Pruning (stripping irrelevant content, citing tools like Provence removing up to ~95% of extraneous text), Context Summarization (condensing history, particularly once contexts exceed ~100k tokens), and Context Offloading (storing information outside the context window via tools, e.g. scratchpad/notepad files).
claim_definition: A practitioner's original taxonomy and framework: Breunig coins and names the four failure-mode terms and the six-tactic vocabulary himself, synthesizing and interpreting third-party empirical findings (Google's own Gemini/Pokemon case study writeup, the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, a Microsoft/Salesforce multi-turn prompting study, and tool benchmarks like Provence) rather than running new experiments of his own.
evidence_category: practitioner anecdote and synthesis, built on top of cited benchmark/empirical results from other named sources (Google, Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, Microsoft/Salesforce study)
reproducibility: The underlying benchmark results Breunig cites (Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, the Microsoft/Salesforce multi-turn study, Google's Gemini Pokemon case study) are each independently published by their own authors and have had varying degrees of independent replication/discussion elsewhere, but Breunig's essays themselves do not publish new code, data, or an eval harness, they aggregate and re-narrate existing public results. The taxonomy/naming itself is not a reproducible claim in the empirical sense; the follow-up essay's tactics were later operationalized (not by Breunig but by LangChain) as runnable notebooks in the langchain-ai/how_to_fix_your_context GitHub repo.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No. No vendor product, platform, or commercial context-engineering offering is promoted in either essay; the task brief and search results identify Breunig as an independent writer with a data-science background (Overture Maps Foundation, Reddit) rather than a vendor selling a context/data/caching platform.
conflict_notes: No internal figure discrepancies were found between the two essays and how they are described in secondary coverage (Simon Willison's summary and LangChain's blog both reproduce the same four failure-mode names, the 39% drop figure, and the o3 98.1-to-64.1 figure consistently). One minor inconsistency across secondary sources: Willison's post is described as highlighting five of the six tactics (omitting explicit mention of RAG in some summarized excerpts) while LangChain's citation and Breunig's own post both list six; this looks like an artifact of how a secondary summary was condensed rather than a real discrepancy in Breunig's content, but it was not resolved against the raw HTML of Willison's post.
relationship: Complicates the simple "prompt engineering is dead" framing by giving it technical teeth: Breunig doesn't just declare context engineering important, he specifies the exact mechanisms (poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash) by which stuffing more context into a prompt backfires, which argues against a naive 'just add more context' reading of the context-engineering trend and for disciplined curation instead. It is more a mechanistic complication/refinement of the narrative than a simple endorsement or contradiction.
derivative_of: Explicitly builds on and extends third-party empirical findings rather than prior framework papers: Google DeepMind's own public writeup of the Gemini 2.5 Pokemon-playing agent, the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard's multi-tool accuracy results, and a Microsoft/Salesforce study on multi-turn vs single-turn prompt performance. The taxonomy and six-tactic framework themselves appear to be Breunig's own coinage/packaging rather than a relabeling of a prior named framework, which is consistent with the task brief's characterization of this as the 'connective tissue' between context-rot benchmark data and the context-engineering discipline label; LangChain's and others' later frameworks are the derivative works, not the reverse.
register: practitioner/engineer, written for people building LLM agents day to day; no enterprise-buyer or academic framing (no abstract, no citations list, informal blog format)
notes: Both essays were fetched and reviewed directly from dbreunig.com. Author's professional background (ex-Overture Maps/Reddit) comes from the task brief and general search context rather than a successfully fetched About/bio page on his own site (that page returned 404), so the specific employment history is not independently confirmed from a primary source in this pass, though it is consistent with how he is described elsewhere (e.g. in commentary by Simon Willison and Armin Ronacher amplifying these posts). No numeric contradiction was found between Breunig's essays and how LangChain, Simon Willison, or Armin Ronacher cite them.
new_angle: article_ideas.md's existing 09-27 entry on 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' cites a different, vendor-sourced statistic (an industry survey claiming 82% of IT/data leaders say prompts alone no longer suffice) and does not reference Breunig, his four-failure-mode taxonomy, or his six-tactic framework by name. This research establishes that the specific vocabulary now used across the industry (context poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash; RAG, tool loadout, quarantine, pruning, summarization, offloading) traces to these two independent, non-commercial essays from June 2025, giving the counterpoint piece a documented, high-confidence origin point to cite against vendors who present the same ideas as their own framework.
